text: The 'filled duration illusion' is standardly stated as: a filled interval is judged longer than an equal empty one. Empirical work complicates this. Which statement best captures the prospective/retrospective asymmetry?
choices: A filled interval feels long both in the moment and in retrospect, because more clock-pulses accumulate and more events are encoded
A filled interval tends to feel short in the moment (attention is drawn away from time) but long in retrospect (many events were encoded in memory)
A filled interval tends to feel long in the moment but short in retrospect, because arousal speeds the internal clock while the memory then fades
Prospective and retrospective estimates coincide, since both are computed by counting accumulated pacemaker pulses
explanation: Prospective and retrospective estimation rely on different mechanisms. Prospectively, an engaging (filled) interval draws attention away from time, so the attentional gate lets fewer pulses accumulate and it feels short; retrospectively, the many events encoded make it be remembered as long — the familiar 'where did the week go?' pattern. Choice 3 describes the empty-interval pattern (long in the moment, short in retrospect); choice 4 is wrong because retrospective estimates draw on the number of remembered events/segments, not on pulse counts.
